Member order offers Acquisition, Temperature ↑ and Temperature ↓. Temperature sorting changes presentation, not dataset identity or acquisition order. Repeated temperatures do not become one averaged measurement.

docs.title: Temperatures and member inclusion
docs.text:
Select a member, edit Override / K, Label or Include, then Apply edit. A blank override uses the next available temperature source. Effective temperature precedence is member override → series override when present → calibrated dataset temperature → nominal acquisition temperature. Values must be finite positive Kelvin; invalid higher-priority values do not silently fall back to nominal metadata. An override does not rewrite acquisition metadata.

Include controls use of a member in the series workflow; excluded members remain loaded. It differs from batch target checkboxes and the VT analysis fit mask. Verify temperatures and conditions before interpreting trends; imported nominal temperature is not evidence of calibration.

docs.title: Compare stacked spectra
docs.text:
Synthetic VT tutorial spectra after phase, baseline and individual TMS referencing. This is display normalization, not a comparison of quantitative integrals or sample concentrations.

Choose VT Series → Stacked Spectra, or Spectrum → VT stacked. Select the series and order, then adjust Spacing × and Normalize display. Only included members are displayed. Each trace retains its own ppm grid; spacing and normalization do not change peak positions, intensities stored as data, or processing history.

Click a trace to activate its existing dataset. Reviewed track-point highlights help navigate existing peaks. Tracks, Analysis and Batch open the corresponding windows. A display order is not a new tracking identity; candidate suggestions currently use acquisition-order continuity.

Before tracking, process/reference and pick peaks in each experiment. Before continuing later, save an NMR session. A .nmrseries exports definitions only; it is not an embedded spectrum/session.

docs.title: Axial and Rhombic PCS
docs.text:
PCS Analyzer uses an axial PCS description as the default model and provides an optional rhombic extension when deviations from effective rotational symmetry need to be considered.

This distinction is particularly useful for coordination complexes that are approximately rotational but not perfectly axially symmetric.

docs.title: Axial model
docs.text:
For the default axial treatment,

\[ \delta_{\mathrm{PCS}} = \frac{10^4}{12\pi} \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}G_{\mathrm{ax}}, \]

where

\[ G_{\mathrm{ax}} = \frac{3\cos^2\theta-1}{r^3}. \]

Only the distance \(r\) and polar angle \(\theta\) are required.

Because the axial tensor is rotationally symmetric around \(z\), the azimuthal angle \(\phi\) does not affect the calculated PCS.

This makes the axial model particularly convenient for approximately rotational molecular geometries and for initial tensor-orientation analysis.

docs.title: Rhombic contribution
docs.text:
When in-plane anisotropy is significant, the full PCS expression is used:

\[ \delta_{\mathrm{PCS}} = \frac{10^4}{12\pi} \left( \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}G_{\mathrm{ax}} + \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}G_{\mathrm{rh}} \right), \]

with

\[ G_{\mathrm{rh}} = \frac{3}{2} \frac{\sin^2\theta\cos(2\phi)}{r^3}. \]

The rhombic contribution therefore depends on both \(\theta\) and \(\phi\).

A non-zero \(\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}\) breaks the rotational equivalence of the \(x\) and \(y\) directions.

docs.title: When to consider rhombicity
docs.text:
The axial approximation is generally useful when:

  • the coordination geometry is approximately rotational,
  • the fitted or calculated tensor is close to axial,
  • the purpose is an initial structure–PCS comparison,
  • the available experimental data do not justify a more highly parameterized model.

Rhombicity may be worth considering when:

  • significant systematic residuals remain after an axial fit,
  • equivalent angular regions show different PCS behavior,
  • computational magnetic-susceptibility calculations predict \(\chi_{xx}\neq\chi_{yy}\),
  • the molecular geometry shows substantial distortion from rotational symmetry,
  • a full susceptibility-tensor analysis is required.

Caution

Improvement after introducing \(\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}\) should not automatically be interpreted as evidence for physical rhombicity.

Structural mismatch, incorrect assignments, non-PCS contributions, conformational averaging, or over-parameterization can produce similar improvements.

docs.title: Active prediction model
docs.text:
The Control Panel's Prediction model selects the ordinary calculated PCS:

Selection Contribution used Axial Δχ_ax G_ax only, even if a rhombic value is stored and enabled Full tensor (Axial + Rhombic) Δχ_ax G_ax plus Δχ_rh G_rh when Enable Δχ_rh is on; otherwise axial only

The stored Δχ_rh value and its enablement are separate from this selection. Choosing Full tensor does not itself enable the rhombic term. Changing the prediction model retains the tensor parameters and experimental observations.

This policy applies to the main-table calculated PCS, linked NMR predictions, Projection Viewer, and 3D PCS field. G_ax vs PCS, Rhombicity Check, and polar contours remain axial diagnostics. The Rhombicity Table separately compares axial and axial-plus-rhombic predictions. Standard nonlinear fitting uses its configured fitted/fixed tensor components; the prediction selector does not replace those fitting choices.

PCS Analyzer can evaluate both the axial-only prediction and the axial–rhombic prediction for the same molecular geometry.

For a nucleus \(i\),

\[ \delta_i^{\mathrm{ax}} = \frac{10^4}{12\pi} \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}G_{\mathrm{ax},i}, \]

whereas

\[ \delta_i^{\mathrm{ax+rh}} = \frac{10^4}{12\pi} \left( \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}G_{\mathrm{ax},i} + \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}G_{\mathrm{rh},i} \right). \]

The difference

\[ \delta_i^{\mathrm{rh}} = \delta_i^{\mathrm{ax+rh}} - \delta_i^{\mathrm{ax}} \]

represents the contribution introduced by the rhombic term.

docs.title: Geometrical factors
docs.text:
PCS Analyzer evaluates the geometrical factors from coordinates already expressed in the tensor frame:

\[ G_{\mathrm{ax}} = \frac{3\cos^2\theta-1}{r^3}, \] \[ G_{\mathrm{rh}} = \frac{3}{2} \frac{\sin^2\theta\cos(2\phi)}{r^3}. \]

The sign and magnitude of the rhombic contribution therefore depend on both the rhombic susceptibility parameter and the position of the nucleus within the \(xy\)-plane.

docs.title: Relation to diagnostics and fitting
docs.text:
The rhombic term can be incorporated in fitting when a full axial–rhombic model is required.

Residual-based diagnostics can also be used to examine whether deviations from an axial model correlate with the rhombic geometrical factor.

These approaches should be interpreted as model diagnostics rather than as proof that a rhombic tensor is uniquely required.

See:

  • PCS Theory
  • Tensor Conventions
  • Residual Analysis
  • Rhombicity Diagnostics

docs.title: PCS Contour Plots
docs.text:
PCS contour plots provide a geometrical representation of the pseudocontact-shift field around the paramagnetic centre.

PCS Analyzer uses these plots primarily to visualize the axial PCS model that forms the default description for approximately rotational coordination geometries.

docs.title: Axial PCS contours
docs.text:
For the axial model,

\[ \delta_{\mathrm{PCS}} = \frac{10^4}{12\pi} \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}} \frac{3\cos^2\theta-1}{r^3}. \]

For a selected PCS value, the corresponding radial coordinate can be written as

\[ r = \left[ \frac{ 10^4\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}} \left(3\cos^2\theta-1\right) }{ 12\pi\delta_{\mathrm{PCS}} } \right]^{1/3}. \]

The resulting contour therefore shows the spatial positions that produce the same axial PCS value for a given \(\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}\).

docs.title: Polar representation
docs.text:
The 2D polar PCS plot displays:

  • \(\theta\) as the angular coordinate,
  • \(r\) as the radial coordinate,
  • PCS values as contour lines,
  • selected nuclei at their corresponding \((\theta,r)\) positions.

Because the default axial model is rotationally symmetric around the \(z\)-axis, the azimuthal coordinate \(\phi\) is not required for this representation.

This makes the polar plot particularly useful for rapidly comparing molecular geometry with an axial PCS field.

docs.title: Sign of the PCS field
docs.text:
The angular factor

\[ 3\cos^2\theta-1 \]

changes sign at approximately

\[ 54.7^\circ. \]

Consequently, the axial PCS field is divided into angular regions of opposite sign.

The sign of the observed PCS additionally depends on the sign of \(\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}\).

docs.title: Rhombic systems
docs.text:
When

\[ \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}\neq0, \]

the PCS becomes dependent on the azimuthal angle \(\phi\):

\[ \delta_{\mathrm{PCS}} = \frac{10^4}{12\pi} \left[ \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}} \frac{3\cos^2\theta-1}{r^3} + \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}} \frac{3}{2} \frac{\sin^2\theta\cos(2\phi)}{r^3} \right]. \]

A single \(r\)-versus-\(\theta\) polar contour can no longer represent the complete three-dimensional PCS field because the field is no longer rotationally invariant around \(z\).

For this reason, the standard 2D polar PCS plot should primarily be interpreted as an axial representation.

Rhombic contributions are better inspected using tensor-aware tables, fitting/diagnostic tools, projection views, or three-dimensional PCS visualization.

Note

The 2D polar PCS plot is intentionally optimized for the axial model used as the default PCS Analyzer workflow.

When rhombicity is included, use the additional rhombic and 3D visualization tools to inspect the full angular dependence.

docs.title: Plot range and interval
docs.text:
The displayed contours are controlled by the selected PCS range and contour interval.

A narrower interval provides more detailed visual resolution but may produce a crowded plot.

For qualitative interpretation, a contour interval that clearly separates positive and negative PCS regions is usually preferable.

docs.title: Half- and quarter-plane angular views
docs.text:
The Half/Quarter plot toggle switches between two polar angular domains:

  • Half-plane view: \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 180^\circ\)
  • Quarter-plane view: \(0^\circ \le \theta \le 90^\circ\)

In the quarter-plane view, positions with \(\theta > 90^\circ\) are folded to \(180^\circ-\theta\). This compact representation is useful for the axially symmetric contour because the axial angular factor is symmetric about \(90^\circ\). Use the half-plane view when the two sides of the tensor \(z\)-axis need to remain visually distinct.

docs.title: Interpreting atom positions
docs.text:
Overlaying nuclei on the PCS contour plot allows direct comparison between molecular geometry and the expected axial PCS field.

Nuclei close to the same contour are expected to have similar axial PCS contributions, provided that the same tensor parameters apply.

Deviations between experimental values and the axial contour expectation can motivate further analysis, including:

  • tensor reorientation,
  • structural refinement,
  • rhombicity analysis,
  • conformational averaging,
  • evaluation of non-PCS contributions.

See Axial and Rhombic PCS for the full model. For the implemented markers, selection, averaging overlays, and exports, see 2D Polar PCS Plot.

docs.title: Tensor Conventions
docs.text:
PCS Analyzer uses an axial–rhombic representation of the magnetic susceptibility tensor.

The software is primarily designed for approximately rotational coordination geometries, so the axial anisotropy is treated as the default PCS parameter. A rhombic component can be included when in-plane anisotropy is significant.

docs.title: Isotropic susceptibility
docs.text:
The isotropic magnetic susceptibility is defined as

\[ \chi_{\mathrm{iso}} = \frac{\chi_{xx}+\chi_{yy}+\chi_{zz}}{3}. \]

When an experimental molar susceptibility is supplied, PCS Analyzer uses

\[ \chi_{\mathrm{iso}}=\chi_{\mathrm{mol}}. \]

docs.title: Axial anisotropy
docs.text:
PCS Analyzer defines the axial susceptibility anisotropy as

\[ \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}} = \chi_{zz} - \frac{\chi_{xx}+\chi_{yy}}{2}. \]

For an axially symmetric tensor,

\[ \chi_{xx}=\chi_{yy}, \]

and \(\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}\) fully describes the anisotropic part relevant to the default PCS model.

docs.title: Rhombic anisotropy
docs.text:
The rhombic susceptibility anisotropy is defined as

\[ \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}} = \chi_{xx}-\chi_{yy}. \]

A non-zero \(\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}\) introduces an in-plane anisotropy and makes the \(x\) and \(y\) tensor directions distinct.

docs.title: Reconstruction of the principal tensor components
docs.text:
Using the definitions above,

\[ \chi_{xx} = \chi_{\mathrm{iso}} - \frac{\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}}{3} + \frac{\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}}{2}, \] \[ \chi_{yy} = \chi_{\mathrm{iso}} - \frac{\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}}{3} - \frac{\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}}{2}, \]

and

\[ \chi_{zz} = \chi_{\mathrm{iso}} + \frac{2\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}}{3}. \]

For the axial case,

\[ \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}=0, \]

so that

\[ \chi_{xx}=\chi_{yy} = \chi_{\mathrm{iso}} - \frac{\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}}{3}, \]

and

\[ \chi_{zz} = \chi_{\mathrm{iso}} + \frac{2\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}}{3}. \]

docs.title: Tensor reconstruction modes
docs.text: PCS Analyzer supports two reconstruction modes.

docs.title: Experimental isotropic susceptibility
docs.text:
If \(\chi_{\mathrm{mol}}\) is available, the program uses

\[ \chi_{\mathrm{iso}}=\chi_{\mathrm{mol}} \]

and reconstructs the full tensor while preserving the isotropic susceptibility.

This mode is appropriate when an experimental molar susceptibility is available and the absolute principal susceptibility values are required.

docs.title: Traceless anisotropic reconstruction
docs.text:
If no isotropic susceptibility is supplied, PCS Analyzer uses

\[ \chi_{\mathrm{iso}}=0. \]

The reconstructed tensor then contains only the anisotropic part:

\[ \chi_{xx} = -\frac{\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}}{3} + \frac{\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}}{2}, \] \[ \chi_{yy} = -\frac{\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}}{3} - \frac{\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}}{2}, \] \[ \chi_{zz} = \frac{2\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}}{3}. \]

This satisfies

\[ \chi_{xx}+\chi_{yy}+\chi_{zz}=0. \]

Note

The traceless reconstruction represents the anisotropic tensor used for PCS analysis and visualization. It does not contain an absolute isotropic susceptibility offset.

docs.title: Coordinate convention
docs.text:
PCS Analyzer evaluates PCS values in the tensor coordinate frame.

  • \(z\): principal axial direction
  • \(x,y\): in-plane principal directions
  • \(\theta\): polar angle relative to \(z\)
  • \(\phi\): azimuthal angle in the \(xy\)-plane

For the axial model, rotation around \(z\) is irrelevant because \(\chi_{xx}=\chi_{yy}\).

For the rhombic model, the orientation of the \(x\) and \(y\) axes matters because the PCS contains a \(\cos(2\phi)\) term.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
PCS Analyzer handles

\[ \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}} \quad\text{and}\quad \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}} \]

in units of

\[ 10^{-32}\,\mathrm{m^3} \]

per molecule.

For tensor reconstruction, molecular susceptibility anisotropies are converted to SI molar susceptibility using Avogadro's constant:

\[ \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax,mol}} = \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}} \times 10^{-32} \times N_{\mathrm A}, \]

and

\[ \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh,mol}} = \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}} \times 10^{-32} \times N_{\mathrm A}, \]

where

\[ N_{\mathrm A} = 6.0221408\times10^{23}\,\mathrm{mol^{-1}}. \]

Thus, an input value of

\[ \Delta\chi = 1.0 \]

corresponds to

\[ 6.0221408\times10^{-9}\,\mathrm{m^3\,mol^{-1}}. \]

When an experimental molar susceptibility is supplied, PCS Analyzer uses it as

\[ \chi_{\mathrm{iso}}=\chi_{\mathrm{mol}}. \]

Warning

Magnetic susceptibility conventions are not universal. Always verify the definitions of \(\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}\), \(\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}\), tensor-axis ordering, and units before comparing parameters obtained from different programs or publications.

CGS susceptibility data

Molar magnetic susceptibilities are often reported in magnetochemistry in cgs units of \(\mathrm{cm^3\,mol^{-1}}\).

These values must be converted to SI before use in PCS Analyzer:

\[ \chi_{\mathrm{mol}}^{\mathrm{SI}} = 4\pi\times10^{-6} \chi_M^{\mathrm{cgs}}. \]

Do not convert cgs susceptibility to SI using only the geometric \(\mathrm{cm^3}\rightarrow\mathrm{m^3}\) factor.

See PCS Theory for the corresponding PCS equations.

For scientific background and the distinction between general methods and the implemented workflows, see Method References.

docs.title: ORCA tensors from PCS Workbench
docs.text: Use the reviewed Tensor Transfer workflow to apply an ORCA-derived anisotropic tensor in the active structure frame. It selects Full tensor and retains source information; it does not replace the experimental molar susceptibility.

docs.title: PCS Theory
docs.text:
PCS Analyzer is primarily designed for coordination complexes with approximately rotational molecular geometry, where the magnetic susceptibility anisotropy can often be described using an effective axial model.

In this default case, the pseudocontact shift is written as

\[ \delta_{\mathrm{PCS}}\;(\mathrm{ppm}) = \frac{10^4}{12\pi} \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}G_{\mathrm{ax}}, \]

with the axial geometrical factor

\[ G_{\mathrm{ax}} = \frac{3\cos^2\theta-1}{r^3}. \]

Here,

  • \(r\) is the distance from the paramagnetic centre to the observed nucleus,
  • \(\theta\) is the polar angle relative to the principal \(z\)-axis,
  • \(\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}\) is the axial magnetic susceptibility anisotropy.

This form provides the default geometrical description used throughout the basic PCS Analyzer workflow.

docs.title: Rhombic extension
docs.text:
For systems in which in-plane anisotropy cannot be neglected, PCS Analyzer can include a rhombic contribution.

The full axial–rhombic expression is

\[ \delta_{\mathrm{PCS}}\;(\mathrm{ppm}) = \frac{10^4}{12\pi} \left( \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}}G_{\mathrm{ax}} + \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}G_{\mathrm{rh}} \right), \]

where

\[ G_{\mathrm{rh}} = \frac{3}{2} \frac{\sin^2\theta\cos(2\phi)}{r^3}. \]

The azimuthal angle \(\phi\) is measured in the tensor \(xy\)-plane.

When

\[ \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}}=0, \]

the full expression reduces to the axial model.

Note

The axial model is the default representation in PCS Analyzer because the software is primarily intended for approximately rotational coordination geometries.

Rhombicity can be introduced when the system shows significant deviation from effective axial symmetry or when a full susceptibility-tensor treatment is required.

docs.title: Geometrical interpretation
docs.text:
The PCS depends strongly on both distance and orientation.

The \(r^{-3}\) dependence causes nuclei close to the paramagnetic centre to experience substantially larger PCS values.

For the axial term, the angular dependence is controlled by

\[ 3\cos^2\theta-1. \]

The axial PCS changes sign at the magic angle,

\[ \theta_{\mathrm{m}} = \arccos\left(\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\right) \approx 54.7^\circ. \]

The rhombic contribution additionally depends on \(\phi\) through \(\cos(2\phi)\), introducing an in-plane angular dependence that is absent from the axial approximation.

docs.title: Coordinate frame
docs.text:
PCS calculations are performed in the magnetic susceptibility tensor frame.

In the default axial treatment:

  • the \(z\)-axis defines the principal axial direction,
  • only \(r\) and \(\theta\) are required,
  • rotation about the \(z\)-axis does not change the calculated axial PCS.

When rhombicity is included:

  • the \(x\) and \(y\) directions become physically distinct,
  • the azimuthal angle \(\phi\) must also be considered,
  • rotation about the \(z\)-axis can change the calculated PCS.

See Tensor Conventions for the susceptibility definitions used by PCS Analyzer.

docs.title: Units used by PCS Analyzer
docs.text:
PCS Analyzer accepts

\[ \Delta\chi_{\mathrm{ax}},\Delta\chi_{\mathrm{rh}} \]

in units of

\[ 10^{-32}\,\mathrm{m^3} \]

per molecule, while structural coordinates are given in Å.

The factor \(10^4\) in the program-level PCS equations accounts for these input units and returns the calculated shift in ppm.

For detailed tensor definitions and reconstruction rules, see Tensor Conventions.

docs.title: Scientific background
docs.text: For the point-dipole expression and its distributed-density extension, see A partial differential equation for pseudocontact shift. The method references provide related literature and reporting guidance. Use this manual's explicit unit and tensor definitions when exchanging numerical values.

docs.title: Calculation & Convergence
docs.text: Use the Calculation tab to choose a temperature and prepare the distributed PCS calculation. Load the ORCA output and matching spin-density grid first; see Overview.

docs.title: Normalization and padding
docs.text:
Normalize density integral scales the non-negative calculation density to the Normalization target, normally 1. Normalization order defaults to Before padding. After padding is available for reproducing the earlier workflow. Older presets without an order setting retain the after-padding behavior; Reset to defaults uses before-padding.

These choices affect the calculation, rather than just its appearance. The original signed density is kept separately for export.

Padding factor defaults to 2. Padding expands the grid around the input density to reduce sensitivity to the finite calculation box. Increasing it also increases memory use and calculation time. A factor of 2 gives five times as many samples along each axis, or 125 times as many voxels. Check the input and memory summary before running a large grid.

docs.title: Padding convergence check
docs.text:
The check compares atom-level PDE PCS values at two padding factors. It is optional and off by default.

  1. Expand Padding convergence check on Calculation.
  2. Enable the check and choose Comparison padding factor, normally 3 when the base factor is 2.
  3. Set Tolerance (ppm). The default 0.01 ppm is a starting value, not a universal accuracy requirement.
  4. Use Run computation to calculate the base result and then check it, or Check current result to check a result already available.
  5. Read the outcome above the result tabs and the details in Summary & diagnostics.

Current UI with illustrative data; the displayed tolerance is an example.

Both calculations use the same density normalization scale. The check reports the maximum absolute difference, RMS difference and worst affected atom, excluding the metal centre. It keeps the base result; it does not replace it with the larger comparison grid.

Status Meaning Not checked No check is recorded for this result. Within tolerance All required atom pairs were compared and the maximum difference meets the chosen tolerance. Above tolerance The maximum difference exceeds the chosen tolerance. Consider a larger base padding or review the grid. Incomplete Some required atom values could not be compared. Do not treat this as a pass. Failed The comparison failed; the successful base result is retained.

This checks sensitivity to padding. It does not establish experimental agreement or validate the density, tensor, grid resolution or physical model.

docs.title: Current results and reproducibility
docs.text:
The summary line describes the recorded result, not settings that have not yet been calculated. Replacing an input file or changing calculation inputs invalidates the result. Display changes can redraw the existing field without recalculating it.

The calculation uses the loaded inputs. If a source file changes outside the application, reload it explicitly. Keep the original inputs, parameter preset and numerical exports together. Export metadata records the calculation conditions and any convergence check; see 3D Data Export.

docs.title: 3D Data Export
docs.text:
Use File → Export 3D data… after calculating a current result. NumPy export is included in this dialog; it no longer has a separate command.

Current export dialog, shown with illustrative data.

docs.title: Choose what to export
docs.text:
1. Choose Data: PCS field, Density used by solver, or Original signed density.
  2. Choose Region: the full calculation grid, the input density region, or custom bounds in Å. Bounds appear only for Custom bounds (Angstrom) and select existing grid samples without resampling.
  3. Choose Volume or Isosurface, then select Format.
  4. For an isosurface, enter its signed Surface isovalue. A surface export contains that single level, not the complete viewer scene.
  5. Open Advanced options if needed, then select Export… and choose a filename.

The original signed density is distinct from the absolute-valued density used for calculation. Exporting it does not change the PDE result.

docs.title: Formats
docs.text:
Export Formats Scalar volume CUBE/CUB, VTI, VTK, OpenDX, MRC/CCP4/MAP, NRRD, NPZ, NPY Single isosurface VTP, PLY, STL, OBJ

For a Python workflow, choose NPY for the selected array or NPZ for an array with associated data. For a regular 3D viewer, choose a volume format that the viewer supports. Mesh formats describe a surface and may not retain all colours or materials.

Every export also writes a JSON sidecar beside the data file. Keep it with the export: it records the field, units, grid, region, calculation conditions and any export smoothing. See File Formats for the reference summary.

docs.title: Advanced options
docs.text:
The section is collapsed initially. Opening or closing it retains the selected values.

  • Precision offers Float32 or Float64 for NPY, NPZ and NRRD. MRC/CCP4/MAP use Float32; the text formats use Float64 precision.
  • Compression is available for NPZ and NRRD.
  • Smooth PCS export applies optional Gaussian smoothing to the exported PCS field. Sigma is in voxels. It leaves the calculation and atom comparison unchanged; the collapsed section indicates when smoothing is on.

These controls appear only when applicable. Export smoothing is separate from Smooth PCS display, which affects the viewer only.

An illustrative surface export; precision and compression controls are hidden for this format.

docs.title: Units and saved data
docs.text:
PCS values remain ppm. CUBE/CUB coordinates, including atoms and grid steps, use Bohr; the other implemented formats use Å. Normalized calculation density is converted to Bohr⁻³ in CUBE. Raw signed density retains its source values, labelled source_units, because the reader does not establish its physical unit. Check the sidecar when exchanging files; see Units.

NPY stores the selected array; its coordinates and conditions are in the sidecar. NPZ also includes grid information and metadata. A full, unsmoothed PCS NPZ additionally retains source/solver arrays and tensor settings. Cropped, smoothed or density exports should not be treated as identical full-result archives.

Export runs in the background. Cancellation takes effect between writing steps and may take time during compression or surface extraction. Test a small export in the intended external application before relying on a large batch. Some readers interpret very small NRRD grids differently; VTI is an alternative.

docs.title: Other outputs
docs.text: Export atom PCS to CSV… writes the atom-level comparison. Export PNG…, slice Save plot..., and tensor Save PNG / Save GIF save images rather than numerical volumes. Parameter presets save settings, not the loaded inputs or a completed Workbench session.

docs.title: PCS Workbench
docs.text:
PCS Workbench 0.1.1 is a separate PCS Analyzer window for comparing a point-dipole PCS model with a PCS field generated from an ORCA-derived spatial density grid. Open it from Modules → PCS Workbench or the PCS Workbench shortcut in the main window.

The Workbench does not import the current main-window structure, tensor, or experimental shifts. It loads its own ORCA output and, for distributed-field calculations, its own spin-density .3d file.

Current Calculation tab and result report, shown with illustrative data.

docs.title: Point-dipole and distributed PCS
docs.text:
The two calculations answer different model questions:

  • Point-dipole PCS applies the traceless rank-2 susceptibility tensor at an automatically selected metal coordinate and evaluates the tensor expression at each ORCA atom.
  • PDE PCS uses the same rank-2 tensor with a three-dimensional density grid in an FFT spectral solver. The resulting field is sampled at the ORCA atom positions by cubic interpolation.

The atom comparison reports

\[ \Delta_{\mathrm{PDE-Point}} = \delta_{\mathrm{PDE}}-\delta_{\mathrm{Point}} \]

in ppm. This difference measures disagreement between these two implemented forward models. It is not an experimental residual and does not by itself identify a bonding mechanism or prove a spin-delocalization interpretation.

The canonical PCS definitions remain in PCS Theory and Tensor Conventions.

docs.title: ORCA output
docs.text:
Use File → Open ORCA output… to select .out or .log. The parser requires both:

  • a recognized CARTESIAN COORDINATES (ANGSTROEM) or (BOHR) block; and
  • at least one susceptibility tensor following a TEMPERATURE/K: record and a Tensor in molecular frame heading.

If several susceptibility sections are found, choose the intended section in the selection dialog. The Workbench does not infer the calculation level automatically. The selected section and its source line appear in the report.

The last coordinate block is used. Bohr coordinates are converted to Å. If several tensors are present, Temperature (K) selects one of the parsed temperatures; a programmatic non-exact request is resolved to the nearest available value, while leaving the selection blank uses the first temperature.

The Workbench displays the raw ORCA tensor as a CGS molar Curie quantity in cm³·K/mol and converts it to Å³ per molecule with

\[ \boldsymbol{\chi} = \frac{4\pi\,10^{24}}{N_\mathrm{A}T} \boldsymbol{\chi}_{\mathrm{raw}}. \]

It then removes the isotropic trace and uses only the traceless rank-2 tensor in both PCS calculations. The ORCA coordinates and Tensor in molecular frame matrix are used in the same molecular frame; the Workbench does not provide an additional tensor rotation control.

docs.title: Spin-density grid
docs.text:
Use File → Open spin density… to select an ORCA simple-grid .3d file. The current reader expects, in order:

  1. a title line;
  2. positive nx ny nz dimensions;
  3. ox oy oz origin;
  4. positive dx dy dz spacing; and
  5. exactly nx × ny × nz scalar samples.

The implementation treats the origin and spacing numbers as Å and performs no length-unit conversion. The grid must therefore already share the ORCA structure's molecular frame and Å coordinate convention.

Current density-sign handling

The .3d loader currently applies an absolute value to every scalar sample before reshaping the grid. The original signed samples are retained separately for export; the solver continues to use the non-negative grid. With Normalize density integral enabled, this non-negative grid is scaled to the requested Normalization target using a nested trapezoidal integral. Confirm that these assumptions match the intended calculation before interpreting the PDE result.

The ORCA file alone is sufficient for tensor information, the tensor-spheroid viewer, and tensor transfer to PCS Analyzer. A spin-density grid is required for ▶ Run computation, the PCS field, slices, isosurfaces, and PDE-versus-point comparison.

docs.title: Calculation workflow
docs.text:
1. Load the ORCA output, inspect the available temperatures and tensor conversion in Results & Information, and select Temperature (K) on the Calculation tab.
  2. Load the matching .3d grid.
  3. Set Padding factor, Normalize density integral, Normalization target, and Normalization order under FFT / PDE Settings. The default order is Before padding. Optionally enable the padding convergence check.
  4. Click ▶ Run computation. The calculation runs in a worker thread; another run is rejected while it is busy.
  5. Review Summary & diagnostics and Atom comparison in Results & Information. The line above these tabs records the result temperature, padding factor, and convergence status. PCS values in Atom comparison use two decimal places; the report and numerical exports retain their existing precision.
  6. Configure Surfaces, then use Open / Refresh Viewer. Changing surface, molecule, camera, or export controls redraws the stored result; use Run computation again after changing calculation inputs.
  7. Use Analysis or Plots for comparison plots and tensor visualization; use Open Oblique PCS Slice… for slices. Use File → Export 3D data… for numerical volume and surface exports.

The metal centre is selected automatically as the first recognized metal element in the ORCA atom order. If none is recognized, atom 1 is used. There is currently no Workbench control to override this choice; enable Show atoms and verify the highlighted centre and atom order before accepting atom-level comparisons.

docs.title: FFT/PDE settings and performance
docs.text:
Padding factor adds that many original-grid lengths on each side of every axis before the FFT. A factor of 2 therefore produces approximately five times as many points along each dimension, or 125 times as many voxels before FFT working arrays are included. Large source grids can require substantial memory and computation time.

PCS Workbench uses pyfftw with available CPU threads when it can be imported and otherwise falls back to numpy.fft. This changes the FFT backend, not the documented model. Changing calculation inputs invalidates the current result; calculate again before exporting. See Calculation & Convergence for normalization, memory use and optional padding checks.

docs.title: 3D field and isosurfaces
docs.text:
The Surfaces tab controls two independent displays:

  • Show spin density surface draws the selected positive Density isovalue (a.u.) from the density used by the solver.
  • Show PCS isosurfaces draws both +level and −level surfaces for every positive ppm row in PCS Isosurface Levels. Each row has positive/negative colors, style, and opacity.

Smooth PCS display (Gaussian) filters a copy of the PCS grid for isosurface rendering only. Its sigma is in voxels. It does not recalculate the stored PCS field or the atom comparison. Export smoothing is a separate, optional setting in Export 3D data. Atom and bond display, bond tolerance, labels, grid, outline, colors, opacity, camera, and projection are also visualization controls rather than PCS inputs.

The following field image illustrates an earlier calculation.

The surface is an interpolated representation of a finite numerical grid. Its apparent smoothness and the chosen isovalue do not increase the precision of the input density or prove a physical boundary.

docs.title: Atom-level comparison
docs.text:
PDE PCS vs Point-dipole PCS… plots point-dipole PCS on the x-axis and interpolated PDE PCS on the y-axis. PDE − Point residuals… plots their signed difference. The plot options can restrict the atom set, minimum absolute PCS or difference, and the largest differences; they can also change color, marker size, labels, and a visual tolerance band.

The displayed RMSD, MAE, mean Δ, and maximum |Δ| summarize the filtered atom rows. They compare two calculations, not calculated values against experimental data.

The following comparison image illustrates an earlier calculation; it is not a new 0.1.1 validation.

docs.title: Oblique slices
docs.text:
Open Oblique PCS Slice… defines a plane through the selected metal using either cartesian_z or the tensor principal z direction and the vector from the metal to a chosen Direction atom. Atom plane tolerance (Å) controls which atom markers are included near the plane; it does not alter the field slice. Contours may use automatic symmetric levels or explicit signed ppm levels.

Slice plots can show Ref/element labels and can be saved as PNG, PDF, or SVG.

The following slice image illustrates an earlier calculation.

docs.title: Tensor spheroid
docs.text:
Tensor spheroid… diagonalizes the traceless rank-2 tensor, draws its principal directions through the selected metal, and scales an ellipsoidal visual aid from the eigenvalue magnitudes. The controls use two columns, with a scrollable settings area and fixed action buttons. The scaling modes are:

  • per_frame, which normalizes each temperature independently;
  • global, which uses a common scale over the selected temperature range; and
  • absolute, which applies the configured absolute display factor.

Only global or a consistently chosen absolute factor supports visual size comparison across temperatures. The spheroid is a tensor visualization, not a spin-density surface or molecular orbital. It can be saved as PNG. Save GIF sweeps the selected ORCA temperature range with a fixed camera and requires the tensor viewer to be open.

Current controls, shown with illustrative data. The animation below is an earlier example.

docs.title: Exports and presets
docs.text:
Command Output Export PNG… PNG of the live current camera when Export view: current succeeds, or an off-screen render using the configured preset, DPI, width, and transparency. File → Export 3D data… PCS or density volumes, including NumPy, or a selected isosurface. See 3D Data Export for formats and options. Export atom PCS to CSV… UTF-8-with-BOM CSV with Ref, element, XYZ, PDE PCS, point PCS, and PDE-minus-point difference. Save preset… / Load preset… JSON containing Workbench calculation, surface, molecule, camera, and PNG controls. It does not contain input files or a computed field. Tensor Save PNG / Save GIF Static spheroid image or temperature-sweep animation. Slice Save plot... PNG, PDF, or SVG contour plot.

The Workbench session and camera snapshot are transient and are not part of the main .pcsp project. A tensor applied to the main Analyzer document, together with its import source, can be saved in that document; see Tensor Transfer. Save the input files, parameter preset, and numerical exports needed to reproduce a result. See File Formats for the concise format reference and Units for the application's general unit conventions.

docs.title: Interpretation limits
docs.text:
• PDE-versus-point differences are model differences, not experimental validation.
  • The solver uses absolute density values and normalization is enabled by default. The original signed samples remain available for export.
  • Metal selection is automatic and should be checked for unusual structures.
  • Grid extent, spacing, padding, normalization, and interpolation affect the numerical result.
  • Display smoothing, surface levels, opacity, colors, and spheroid scale affect presentation only.
  • Neither an isosurface, a slice, nor a tensor spheroid uniquely establishes bonding, delocalization, or a physical mechanism.

docs.title: Tensor Transfer
docs.text: Send tensor to PCS Analyzer… brings the selected ORCA susceptibility anisotropy into the active Analyzer document. It does not transfer a distributed PCS field or experimental shifts.

docs.title: Before starting
docs.text:
Open PCS Workbench from PCS Analyzer and load an ORCA output. A spin-density grid and PDE calculation are not required. The command is disabled in a standalone Workbench.

The active Analyzer document must contain the same structure with matching atom order and the corresponding assigned metal centre. A rigid rotation or translation is allowed; a changed conformation, different atom order or incompatible centre is not. Automatic atom matching is not provided.

docs.title: Review and apply
docs.text:
1. Select Temperature (K) in the Workbench.
  2. Click Send tensor to PCS Analyzer… beneath the temperature controls, or use the same File-menu command.
  3. Review the source, temperature, target document, current/imported tensor and structure agreement.
  4. Confirm matching atom order, then select Apply. Cancel leaves the Analyzer tensor unchanged.
  5. Review the main Tensor state and Details. Use document Undo to revert the import; Redo restores it.

Current review window with illustrative data. Apply is disabled until atom order is confirmed.

The transfer expresses the anisotropic tensor in the target structure's frame and selects Full tensor (Axial + Rhombic). It retains the target structure and assigned centre. Experimental shifts and experimental molar susceptibility are unchanged. A working fit preview is cleared, while recorded fit results remain available.

If the target document or its inputs change during review, open a new preview. Apply or discard an active conformer preview before importing. A rejected transfer is a reason to check the structures and order, not to bypass the checks.

docs.title: Source information and saving
docs.text:
The existing Tensor state shows ORCA and the selected temperature. Subsequent physical edits can show Modified from ORCA. Details displays the import source and retains access to the Rhombicity Table. Without an ORCA source, Details keeps its usual Rhombicity Table navigation.

Save the Analyzer document as .pcsp to retain the applied tensor and its source information. This does not save the Workbench's loaded files, density grid, result or camera state. Keep the source ORCA output separately. See Projects and Persistence and Tensor Conventions.

docs.title: Creating Plugins
docs.text:
This is plugin-author reference. For installing and running existing tools, see Module Manager.

The installer accepts a single Python file or a folder/ZIP package. In each case the installed entry module must define:

def register(app):
    ...

register(app) is called while external plugins are loaded for the Modules menu. It should register commands and return promptly; launch the actual tool only from a deferred callback.

docs.title: Single-file plugins
docs.text:
A .py plugin must define both PLUGIN_INFO as a dictionary and register(app):

PLUGIN_INFO = {
    "id": "evans_calculator",
    "name": "Evans Method Calculator",
    "version": "0.1.0",
    "author": "Author Name",
    "description": "Calculate magnetic susceptibility from Evans method data.",
    "type": "window",
    "standalone": True,
    "dependencies": [],
}


def open_plugin(app):
    ...


def register(app):
    app.register_tool(
        tool_id="evans_calculator.open",
        label="Evans Method Calculator...",
        command=lambda: open_plugin(app),
        category="Plugins",
    )

During installation PCS Analyzer imports the selected file to inspect PLUGIN_INFO. Import-time code therefore runs before the user can use the plugin. The installer validates the ID, version and declared compatibility, copies the file to plugins/installed/<plugin_id>/plugin.py, and generates a manifest from selected PLUGIN_INFO fields. New installations are enabled; replacements retain the existing enabled state.

docs.title: Folder-based plugins
docs.text:
bleaney_vt/
├─ manifest.json
├─ plugin.py
├─ plugin_ui/
├─ plugin_logic/
├─ resources/
└─ examples/

The selected folder may contain manifest.json directly, or it may contain one immediate child folder that does. The entry named by the manifest must exist. Package-style relative imports are supported:

from .plugin_ui.main_window import MyWindow
from .plugin_logic.fitting import run_fit

The ZIP installer accepts the same layout after extraction. See Distribution and installation before sharing a ZIP, especially its current security limitations.

docs.title: Registering a deferred command
docs.text:
Use register_tool() for a launcher that can be pinned in Quick tools; add a Modules command separately with add_menu_item() when desired. Give each launcher a unique stable ID to avoid replacing another tool. The legacy add_menu_item() pattern below remains supported but does not itself create a pinnable tool. See PluginApp.

def open_plugin(app):
    from .plugin_ui.main_window import BleaneyWindow
    return BleaneyWindow(app.root, app=app)


def register(app):
    app.add_menu_item(
        label="Bleaney / VT Shift Fitting...",
        command=lambda: open_plugin(app),
    )

Do not write command=open_plugin(app): that calls the function during registration instead of when the user selects the menu item.

docs.title: Import-time safety
docs.text:
A plugin should not open windows, call main() or mainloop(), start calculations, launch subprocesses, load large data, or modify application state merely because it was imported. PCS Analyzer cannot enforce this rule or reverse import-time side effects.

Move optional or expensive imports into the launch function where practical, and keep standalone execution guarded:

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run_standalone()

docs.title: GUI integration
docs.text: For a Tkinter plugin launched inside PCS Analyzer, use tk.Toplevel(app.root) when practical. Do not create a second tk.Tk() root or start another event loop. A genuinely standalone path may create its own root only inside the guarded standalone entry point.

docs.title: Dependencies and resources
docs.text:
Manifest dependency fields are metadata only in the current host. The manager neither installs nor checks them, so plugin code must detect required and optional packages and report missing ones clearly.

Resolve resources relative to the plugin file rather than the process working directory:

from pathlib import Path

PLUGIN_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
RESOURCE_DIR = PLUGIN_DIR / "resources"

docs.title: Development checklist
docs.text:
1. Give the plugin a stable ID and define register(app).
  2. Keep import and registration lightweight.
  3. Use deferred menu callbacks.
  4. Prefer the documented PluginApp helpers to raw state access.
  5. Handle unavailable dependencies in plugin code.
  6. Install through Module Manager; restart after every update or replacement.
  7. Verify that the plugin is both listed and successfully loaded.
  8. Exercise enable, disable, removal, and reinstall behavior with disposable test data.
  9. Test standalone mode separately if the plugin claims to support it.

docs.title: Plugin Installation and Distribution
docs.text: For routine use, follow Module Manager. Browse and Updates use the configured catalog; Installed also accepts trusted local packages. These workflows validate new manifests and application compatibility. They do not resolve Python dependencies or sandbox code.

docs.title: Accepted local packages
docs.text:
Action in Installed Package Install .py Plugin A Python file defining a PLUGIN_INFO dictionary and callable register(app). Inspection imports the file; the installed entry is copied as plugin.py with a generated manifest. Install Folder A folder containing manifest.json and its declared entry. A wrapper containing only one immediate package folder is also accepted. Install ZIP The same package layout archived as a ZIP, at the root or inside one wrapper folder. Ambiguous multi-package layouts are rejected.

A practical package is:

my_tool/
├─ manifest.json
├─ plugin.py
├─ resources/
└─ examples/

Entries must stay within the package. Unsafe archive paths, symlinks and unsupported archive entries are rejected; extraction is staged before installation. Keep IDs stable and use versions understood by PCS Analyzer (see Manifest). New installs are enabled, while replacement preserves an existing plugin's enabled state.

docs.title: Catalog installation
docs.text:
Refresh Catalog reads available releases and their compatibility/lifecycle metadata. Install or Update downloads the selected package, verifies SHA-256 and checks that its manifest ID/version matches the catalog release before installation. A hash mismatch, download error or invalid package is reported through Last operation details. No update is installed automatically.

Local folder/ZIP/file installation does not independently authenticate its source or require a catalog hash. Catalog integrity checks are not signatures or a security/scientific review of the code.

docs.title: Replacement and removal behavior
docs.text:
Installation is prepared before replacing live files. Replacement uses a backup; on failure the installer attempts to restore the previous files and registry. Removal likewise preserves a recoverable copy until its record change succeeds. If rollback or cleanup fails, warnings identify remaining recovery paths. Read those details, preserve backups and restart before recovery; do not delete reported folders blindly.

An updated version on disk is not necessarily the code running in this session. Restart after updating or replacing a plugin, including local reinstallations. Enable/disable or Refresh is not a substitute for a clean restart. See Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Author distribution checklist
docs.text:
• Supply the required manifest, or equivalent PLUGIN_INFO for a single-file plugin; define register(app) in the declared entry.
  • Use a stable lowercase ID and consistent release/manifest versions.
  • Keep import and registration lightweight; defer tool launch to a callback.
  • State required dependencies and supported PCS Analyzer versions. Dependency declarations are informational; handle missing packages in the plugin.
  • Resolve resources relative to the plugin directory and include their licenses.
  • Test clean startup, successful loading, enable/disable, replacement and removal.
  • For catalog distribution, provide the release ZIP, its SHA-256 and matching metadata. A developer release alone does not change the catalog.

The distribution notes describe repository responsibilities and the limits of the current interface.

docs.title: Plugin Manifest Reference
docs.text: This is plugin-author reference. Users should normally manage modules through Module Manager, rather than editing installed metadata. Folder/ZIP packages provide manifest.json; single-file installation generates one from PLUGIN_INFO.

docs.title: Minimal practical manifest
docs.text:
{
  "schema_version": 1,
  "id": "my_tool",
  "name": "My Tool",
  "version": "1.0.0",
  "entry": "plugin.py",
  "min_app_version": "1.3.4"
}

docs.title: Current field behavior
docs.text:
Field New-package requirement or behavior id Required; matches ^[a-z][a-z0-9_]*$. It is the installation identity. New installation does not normalize arbitrary names into valid IDs. Reusing the ID replaces that plugin. name Required nonempty display name. version Required nonempty PEP 440 version; compared as a parsed version rather than plain text. Semantic-style MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH is recommended. entry Required nonempty relative path to an existing file inside the package; traversal and unsafe paths are rejected. The module must provide register(app). schema_version Optional; when supplied must be integer 1. min_app_version, max_app_version Optional valid version strings; inclusive application-version bounds checked at installation. Minimum must not exceed maximum. author, description, type, standalone, license Descriptive metadata; type/standalone do not select a different host API. dependencies, optional_dependencies Descriptive; no dependency installation or resolution. category Optional functional category for Ribbon icons. Use NMR / PCS, Structure, Visualization, or Other / Uncategorized. Missing/unrecognized values use the generic icon. state_access Descriptive intent only; no permission enforcement. api_version, entry_function No API negotiation or alternate entry function is implemented. The host calls register(app). enabled Not the enabled-state control. Enable/Disable is application-managed in Module Manager.

Unknown fields may remain in the supplied manifest without being acted on. Legacy aliases such as requires and optional_requires are not dependency resolution mechanisms. Catalog category/source links belong to catalog metadata; do not assume every manifest field appears in Browse.

docs.title: Single-file PLUGIN_INFO
docs.text: Supply a valid id, name, version and a callable register(app). The generated manifest uses entry: plugin.py. It copies author, description, standalone and dependencies, plus supplied schema version, type, optional dependencies, application-version bounds, license and category. Other keys are not necessarily copied. Single-file inspection executes Python code.

docs.title: Legacy installed plugins
docs.text:
Loading an already installed legacy manifest is more permissive than installing a new package. Its omitted entry can default to plugin.py; a manifest/installed ID disagreement is reported as a warning. Valid application-version bounds are checked, while malformed bounds may be ignored with diagnostics. New installs must satisfy the stricter validation above. Inspect Session status → Details after updating old packages; do not interpret legacy acceptance as API stability.

Changing a public ID creates a different installation identity. Keep IDs and release metadata consistent, and see Creating Plugins for a working entry pattern.

docs.title: Module Manager
docs.text:
Open Modules → Module Manager... or Tools Ribbon → Modules → Module Manager to browse and manage external Python plugins. Built-in tools such as PCS Workbench ship with PCS Analyzer and are not removed through this manager. Most external modules are standalone tools launched from the host; they do not imply a mature, versioned extension API.

Module Manager — Browse view.

docs.title: Launching and arranging modules in the Ribbon
docs.text:
The Tools → Modules group keeps Module Manager above Arrange modules…, beside launchers from enabled modules that loaded successfully. Up to three launchers appear directly; additional commands are under More. A module may contribute multiple commands. The original Modules menu remains available.

Direct launcher buttons are limited to 240 logical pixels including their icons. Long names are shortened with an ellipsis using the current font and display scale. Hover for the full name; the ordering dialog also retains full labels. The three launchers share one column width. Shortening changes only presentation, not the module identity, saved order or command that is launched.

Choose Arrange modules… to open Arrange ribbon modules. Drag a row, or select it and use ↑ / ↓. Apply updates the Ribbon; Cancel discards changes since the last Apply. Restore default restores name order in the draft; use Apply to accept it. Additional new commands are appended after your saved order. Unavailable commands consume no Ribbon slots. The arrangement is saved in application settings, not in a .pcsp, and does not reorder the original Modules menu or Quick tools.

Icons use four functional categories: NMR / PCS, Structure, Visualization, and Other / Uncategorized. Missing or unrecognized category metadata uses the generic icon. Categories do not force the order.

docs.title: Browse, Installed and Updates
docs.text:
View What to do Browse Inspect catalog descriptions, versions, categories and status. Select a module for Details, Repository or Homepage where supplied. Install is offered for an eligible uninstalled module; Update for an eligible newer release. Refresh Catalog retrieves current catalog metadata. Installed Inspect local versions, enabled state and Session status. Install a local .py, folder or ZIP; enable, disable or remove a selected module. Details shows its session diagnostics and Refresh rereads local state. Updates Review compatible newer catalog versions, select a module, read Details and choose Update. Updates are explicit; opening the manager does not install them. Other states Inspect reasons for incompatible, deprecated, unavailable, blocked, local-only or local-error entries. These are not additional installable releases.

Catalog access requires an internet connection. A failed fetch is reported; local installations remain available. Local-only means absent from the current catalog, not necessarily broken. A catalog classification is separate from whether code loaded successfully in this session.

docs.title: Install, update and remove
docs.text:
1. Read the selected module's description, compatibility and source information.
  2. Choose Install or Update, or use a local install action in Installed.
  3. Review the security confirmation. Wait for completion and read any warning; Last operation details explains failures and recovery paths.
  4. Check Installed → Session status and Details, then launch its available Modules command or pin a registered tool launcher in Control Panel → Quick tools → Customize Tools.

New installations and enable/disable actions refresh the Modules menu. Restart PCS Analyzer after an update or replacement to execute the new code: a menu refresh can still use the previously imported version. Disabling or removing a plugin does not close its windows or undo arbitrary Python side effects; restart for a clean session.

Remove asks for confirmation and removes installed files and their record. Keep any plugin-specific data separately before removal. If an operation cannot finish or cleanup is incomplete, use its reported details rather than assuming that either the old or new version is active.

docs.title: Compatibility and recovery
docs.text:
New installations validate the plugin ID, version, manifest, entry path and declared application-version bounds. Catalog downloads additionally check the published SHA-256 and expected package ID/version. Invalid, incompatible or unsafe packages are rejected before replacement. This does not install Python dependencies or prove scientific correctness.

Replacement is staged with a recoverable backup and attempted rollback on failure. Files locked on Windows, rollback errors or cleanup failures can require a restart and leave recovery paths. Preserve those paths, close plugin windows, restart and follow Troubleshooting; recovery is not guaranteed if filesystem operations fail.

docs.title: Session diagnostics
docs.text:
Installed, enabled and loaded are different states. Session status can show Loaded, Disabled, Skipped, Failed, a warning, or Not loaded in this session. Details provides the load phase, error, missing dependency, warnings and technical traceback when available. One plugin's load failure is reported without intentionally preventing other plugins from loading. Runtime failures inside a launched tool may need to be reported to its author.

Legacy installed manifests are loaded more permissively than new packages: valid version bounds are checked, but malformed compatibility metadata can be ignored with a warning. A successful load with such a warning is not evidence of declared compatibility.

docs.title: Security boundary
docs.text:
Trusted code only

Plugins execute Python with PCS Analyzer's permissions and are not sandboxed. Even inspection of a local .py file executes its import-time code. SHA-256 verifies integrity against catalog metadata, not safety, authorship or scientific correctness. Install only code you trust.

See Installation and distribution for package choices and Plugin author reference for development. The current PluginApp is unversioned; a stable integrated API remains future work.

docs.title: PluginApp Reference
docs.text:
This page is for plugin authors; Module Manager covers end-user installation and diagnostics.

The current PluginApp object is a small convenience wrapper around the application's shared state. It is unversioned, exposes mutable internals, and should not be treated as a stable or mature public extension API.

PCS Analyzer calls exactly one plugin entry point:

def register(app):
    ...

The manifest cannot select a different function.

docs.title: Implemented surface
docs.text:
Member Current behavior app.root Returns state["root"], normally the Tk root. app.state The raw, mutable shared state dictionary. register_tool(tool_id, label, command, *, category="Plugins", enabled=None, order=0, tooltip="") Registers a deferred launcher for Quick tools pinning and, during successful plugin registration, the Tools Ribbon; does not itself add a menu item; returns a ToolLauncher. enabled, when supplied, is a callable predicate. Use a unique stable tool ID. add_menu_item(label, command, menu="Modules") Adds a command to a named host menu; raises if the menu is unavailable. Modules-menu commands registered by successfully loaded plugins also appear in the Tools Ribbon. add_separator(menu="Modules") Adds a separator when the named menu exists. get_current_structure() Returns atom_data_eff, falling back to atom_data. get_raw_structure() Returns atom_data_raw, falling back to atom_data. get_delta_exp_values() Returns a shallow dictionary copy of delta_exp_values, or an empty dictionary. get_pcs_values_by_id() Returns a shallow dictionary copy of pcs_by_id, or an empty dictionary. get_metal_position() Returns (x0, y0, z0) converted to floats, defaulting missing coordinates to zero. refresh_views() Attempts the registered update_graph() and plot_cartesian(state) callbacks. Exceptions from either callback are currently suppressed.

Return values are current application data structures, not frozen public models. Accessors that return dictionaries make only shallow copies.

docs.title: Registering a tool launcher
docs.text:
def register(app):
    app.register_tool(
        tool_id="my_tool.open",
        label="My Tool...",
        command=lambda: open_plugin(app),
        category="Plugins",
        tooltip="Open My Tool",
    )

Users can pin registered launchers through Quick tools → Customize Tools. Add a menu command separately with add_menu_item() when needed. Registration creates a launcher, not a scientific-data service or a permission boundary. A repeated tool ID replaces that registered launcher, so avoid IDs belonging to other plugins.

Ribbon icon categories are NMR / PCS, Structure, Visualization, and Other / Uncategorized. An explicit launcher category takes precedence over the manifest category; the default Plugins uses the manifest category, then the generic fallback. Legacy PCS / Dynamics and Structure Analysis map to NMR / PCS and Structure icons respectively. Existing free-text category values remain valid. Ribbon order is controlled by the user, independently of the order value used by the Quick tools registry.

Modules-menu-only registration is supported without modifying existing modules. Separators and commands targeting other menus are not Ribbon launchers. Reusing the same callback object through both registration methods produces one Ribbon entry; separate callback objects are separate commands. Keep launcher IDs and legacy menu labels stable to retain the user's saved arrangement.

docs.title: Registering a menu entry
docs.text:
def open_plugin(app):
    ...


def register(app):
    app.add_menu_item(
        label="My Plugin...",
        command=lambda: open_plugin(app),
    )

The deferred callback prevents the tool from opening while PCS Analyzer imports and registers plugins.

docs.title: Reading data
docs.text:
Prefer the named helpers when they cover the required data:

def open_plugin(app):
    structure = app.get_current_structure()
    delta_exp = app.get_delta_exp_values()
    metal_xyz = app.get_metal_position()

The manifest value state_access is descriptive only. It does not limit access, and app.state remains publicly reachable and writable. Raw state keys, widget references, callbacks, and value shapes can change without a Plugin API compatibility guarantee. A plugin that mutates them can invalidate caches, bypass refresh paths, or corrupt scientific state.

docs.title: GUI integration and errors
docs.text: Use tk.Toplevel(app.root) for Tkinter child windows and do not start a second mainloop() inside PCS Analyzer. Report plugin workflow errors at the plugin UI boundary. Import and register(app) exceptions are caught by the host loader and recorded as load failures, but errors raised later by a plugin command remain the plugin's responsibility.

docs.title: Future direction
docs.text:
A future integrated Plugin API is intended to sit on stable application services, make units and conventions explicit, and expose narrower read-only capabilities before writable ones. That is design direction only. Current plugins must not assume API version negotiation, capability permissions or schema stability. Manifest application-version checks are implemented, but they are separate from API compatibility guarantees.

See Creating Plugins for the current entry pattern and the distribution design notes for distribution responsibilities and current interface limits.

docs.title: Installed but absent from the Modules menu
docs.text:
Open Module Manager → Installed. Check Enabled, Session status and Details. Installed means files/metadata are present, not that registration succeeded. Details can identify missing entry files, dependencies, incompatible versions, import failures or register(app) errors, with technical context. A plugin may register a Quick tools launcher through register_tool() rather than only adding a direct menu entry.

Enable a disabled plugin, then inspect the new session status. Successful local file/folder/ZIP installations now refresh the Modules menu. For a replacement, restart first: a menu refresh may reuse old imported code.

docs.title: Catalog or download fails
docs.text: Read Last operation details for the network, metadata, compatibility, package-ID/version or SHA-256 error. Check the internet connection and retry Refresh Catalog when appropriate. A failed fetch does not remove local modules; a previously loaded catalog may remain visible. Do not bypass a hash mismatch by assuming the package is safe. Check the release with its maintainer.

docs.title: Incompatible, blocked or local-only
docs.text: Use Details to read the reason. Incompatible bounds prevent new installation and valid declared bounds also affect loading. Blocked/unavailable/deprecated catalog entries are not offered as normal install/update actions. Local-only means the installed ID is absent from that catalog; it is not a load diagnosis. Legacy compatibility warnings deserve review even when Session status is Loaded.

docs.title: Refresh does not activate an updated version
docs.text: Installed Refresh rereads local records/diagnostics; Refresh Catalog retrieves catalog metadata. Neither unloads Python modules. After an update or replacement, close plugin windows and restart PCS Analyzer to execute the new files. Disabling/removing also does not reverse arbitrary runtime side effects.

docs.title: Replacement or removal fails on Windows
docs.text: Close plugin windows and restart before retrying. File locks or permissions can prevent replacement, rollback or cleanup. Last operation details reports restart requirements and recovery paths. Preserve those paths and the message; a failed operation is not a guarantee that rollback completed. Avoid deleting an installation or backup manually until the application is closed and the reported state is understood.

docs.title: Registry cannot be read
docs.text: Malformed registry JSON or invalid records are reported as errors rather than silently treated as an empty installed list. Preserve the registry file before repair and provide its error details to the maintainer. Do not reinstall all modules merely because a damaged registry cannot be displayed.

docs.title: Missing dependency
docs.text: Manifest dependency lists are not installed automatically. Follow the plugin's instructions for the Python environment running PCS Analyzer. Frozen builds may need a plugin-specific distribution strategy. Report the missing package from Installed Details to the plugin author.

docs.title: Author checks
docs.text:
• Tool opens during startup: defer launch with command=lambda: open_plugin(app); keep standalone execution behind if __name__ == "__main__".
  • Relative import fails: test the installed package layout, including sibling modules, rather than executing the entry file directly.
  • Resource missing: resolve resource paths relative to Path(__file__).resolve().parent, not the process working directory.
  • One plugin fails while others load: load-error isolation is expected, but import-time state changes are not a sandbox or rollback boundary. Restart before diagnosis; later tool errors remain the plugin's responsibility.

See Creating Plugins, Manifest and the API reference for author-specific details.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
The application version recorded by this repository is PCS Analyzer 1.4.0. The separate module versions are PCS Workbench 0.1.1 and NMR Workbench 0.1.0.

For published packages and release assets, use the PCS Analyzer releases page.

docs.title: PCS Workbench 0.1.1 — unreleased
docs.text:
• Added optional padding convergence checks and clearer recorded result conditions.
  • Added ORCA tensor transfer to the active Analyzer document, with review, Undo/Redo and saved source information.
  • Expanded volume and surface export formats, including CUBE and NumPy, through one Export 3D data… dialog with optional advanced settings.
  • Made before-padding normalization the default while retaining after-padding and compatibility with older presets.
  • Corrected padded-grid coordinates and FFT handling. Recalculating older PDE results can change numerical values; the point-dipole model is unchanged.
  • Improved input/result consistency, background work and dialog layouts.

See PCS Workbench for the updated workflow. These notes describe the current source; published assets are listed separately.

docs.title: Added
docs.text:
• Ribbon toolbar, multiple document tabs and a reorganized Control Panel.
  • Document Undo/Redo with a history dropdown for structure loading, PCS data, tensor and orientation edits, and supported fit/conformer result applications.
  • Shared, adjustable residual-color thresholds for the main and Rhombicity tables, saved with each project.
  • Multi-Conformer fitting with structure mapping, fixed or fitted populations, and bootstrap/cross-validation reliability diagnostics.
  • Joint PCS+RDC fitting and proton Γ₂ PRE fitting.
  • Multi-Lanthanide analysis with independent tensor fits, Reilley separation, coefficient tables and diagnostic plots.
  • NMR Workbench spectrum processing, peak assignments and PCS preparation, plus variable-temperature batch processing, peak tracking and shift analysis.
  • Chemical Map for editing molecular diagrams and linking NMR assignments.
  • Workspace and NMR session saving, and project restoration of Mode C geometry previews and Conformer Search candidates.
  • Module Manager online browsing, installation and updates; module launchers and customizable module ordering in the Tools Ribbon.
  • Help-menu documentation access (F1) and a keyboard-shortcut reference.

docs.title: Improved
docs.text:
• More consistent light/dark themes, additional color palettes and support for larger UI fonts. Theme palettes replace the separate Accent setting.
  • Faster document switching and smoother Ribbon transitions, with improved tab navigation, spacing and overflow controls.
  • Clearer G_ax and Rhombicity diagnostics, collapsible Fit settings, resizable result/plot areas and recorded fit conditions.
  • Uncertainty-weighted fitting and Fit History for reviewing results.
  • The default 3D Structure Viewer now uses PyVista, with linked atom selection, appearance and lighting controls, camera presets and PCS legends. Added figure previews, size/DPI controls and image export; PDF/SVG exports are image-based. The legacy Matplotlib viewer remains available.
  • Updated tutorials and screenshots, with additional fitting, Conformer Search, NMR and visualization examples.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Incorrect tensor orientation when importing main-window settings into Conformer Search. Earlier searches using nonzero orientations should be rerun.
  • Incorrect angular-drift summaries for fixed atoms at the metal centre in Conformer Search.
  • Bond tolerance having no effect in the PCS Field Viewer.

• Corrected the PCS Workbench isotropic-susceptibility calculation.
  • Reorganized PCS Workbench controls and improved interaction with its PyVista viewer.
  • Added Workbench camera presets, projection modes, view save/restore, and improved PNG export.
  • Reorganized the PyVista 3D structure controls and added bond appearance, hydrogen visibility, camera, view-preservation, and PNG-export controls.
  • Corrected symmetry-averaged PCS calculations to average geometrical factors rather than evaluate them only at averaged coordinates.
  • Added rotational ensemble averaging for detected planar ring systems, including configurable sampling, averaged-coordinate visualization, and optional reference overlays.

• Added the main menu bar, Settings window, font options, and revised main control panel.
  • Added the Modules menu and the local Module Manager.
